subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: I'm Francis, Sarita's classmate, and we've shared a bench since Class 6. This year her week is school till two, maths tuition till five, physics coaching till eight, and dance on Saturdays. She eats lunch while copying notes. Last month she stopped laughing at anything. When I asked about the weekend she said, flatly, 'What weekend?' Once she pushed her textbook away and muttered that she hated all of it. Then her mother suggested she drop dance for a term, and Sarita kept Saturday afternoons empty: she lay on the terrace, read comics, walked to the lake with her cousin. Now she answers in physics quicker than before. I can't be sure what changed inside, but her laugh is back.

qa.q: Until what time is Sarita's physics coaching?
qa.a: Till eight.

qa.q: How was Sarita feeling when she said, 'What weekend?'
qa.a: She felt flat and resentful, worn out by a week with no room to rest.

qa.q: What change helped Sarita, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Saturday afternoons free for the terrace, comics and walks gave her mind room to recover, and she seemed sharper in class.

qa.q: How does Francis see the change in Sarita?
qa.a: Francis can't know what changed inside her, but notices that her laugh is back and that she answers quicker in physics.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teenager packed with school, tuition and activities who feels flat and resentful until free time is built into the week.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: Monday, June: Indu's alarm rang at five. School, then chemistry tuition, then entrance coaching, then an online mock test late at night. By Thursday she was crying over a spilled bottle of ink, heart racing, sure she was falling behind everyone. Sunday, a week later: her sister Payal sat down with her and the timetable. 'Where's the part where you just exist?' Indu couldn't find one. Together they crossed out the late mock test and wrote FREE across Wednesday evening. Wednesday, three weeks on: Indu sat on the balcony with Payal, shelling peas and humming, doing nothing important. In Thursday's test she remembered a formula she had been fighting with for days. 'Huh,' she told Payal. 'It stuck.'

qa.q: What did Indu and Payal write across Wednesday evening?
qa.a: FREE.

qa.q: What was Indu worried about when she cried over the spilled ink?
qa.a: She felt anxious and was sure she was falling behind everyone, with no time left to rest.

qa.q: Which step was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Crossing out the late mock test and keeping Wednesday evening free, because the rest gave her mind room to recover and even helped a formula stick.

qa.q: How does Payal seem to see Indu's timetable?
qa.a: Payal sees that it has no space for Indu simply to be, and treats free time as necessary rather than wasted.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a packed schedule of school, tuition and coaching who feels anxious and flat, and recovers once free time is built into the week.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: Felix's week in Hamburg ran like a train timetable: school until three, maths tutoring, swim squad at six, violin on Tuesdays and Thursdays, homework until eleven. By November he felt flat, like a phone stuck at five per cent. He snapped at his mother about a missing sock and cried in the shower without knowing why. His friend Siddiq asked, 'When did you last just do nothing?' Felix couldn't remember. That weekend he asked his parents to drop one tutoring session and keep Sunday afternoons empty. His mother said, 'Rest isn't wasted. It's when your brain sorts out the week.' The first empty Sunday he felt guilty. By the third he was cycling along the river with Siddiq, his head clear again.

qa.q: What did Felix ask his parents for?
qa.a: To drop one tutoring session and keep Sunday afternoons empty.

qa.q: How was Felix feeling by November?
qa.a: He felt flat and drained, like a phone stuck at five per cent, and so strained that he cried without knowing why.

qa.q: Why was the empty Sunday worth protecting?
qa.a: Free time let Felix recover and his brain sort out the week, so his head felt clear again.

qa.q: What did Siddiq notice that Felix had missed?
qa.a: Siddiq saw that Felix never had time to do nothing and cared enough to ask about it.

grounding: A teenager with a packed schedule feels flat and resentful until free time is built into his week.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: At the coaching centre in Kota, Farhan's day began at six with a test and ended at ten with doubt sessions. In between came school, lectures and a hostel study hour. By the second month he sat in the counsellor's room staring at the floor. 'I'm not sad exactly,' he told Alka Ma'am. 'I just feel nothing. And angry at everyone.' Alka Ma'am looked at his timetable. 'Where's your time to breathe?' There wasn't any. Together they found two gaps: Sunday morning off, and forty minutes after dinner for football or a walk. 'Your brain files away what you learnt while you rest,' she said. Farhan doubted it. Two weeks later he admitted his mock score had gone up.

qa.q: What two gaps did Farhan and Alka Ma'am find?
qa.a: Sunday morning off, and forty minutes after dinner for football or a walk.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he said 'I just feel nothing'?
qa.a: He felt numb and resentful, worn down by a timetable with no space to rest.

qa.q: How did Alka Ma'am support Farhan?
qa.a: She looked at his timetable with him, built in real breaks and explained that rest helps the brain file away learning.

qa.q: What would change if Farhan kept the old timetable?
qa.a: He would likely keep feeling numb and angry, and his learning might suffer instead of improving.

grounding: A teenager with no free time feels numb and angry, and a counsellor helps him build rest into the week.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage:
Dear Saurabh Bhaiya,
You asked on the phone why I sounded so dull. Honestly, my week has no gaps. School till two, chemistry tuition, then maths coaching, dance on three evenings, homework after dinner. Even Sunday has a test series. I used to love dance. Now I dread it, and I snap at Mumma when she asks if I've eaten. Last night I stared at my physics book for an hour and nothing went in.
Could you help me talk to Papa? I want to drop the Sunday test series and keep that afternoon free. Not to waste it, just to sleep, read a story, go cycling. You always said your best ideas came on lazy Sundays.
Mahima

qa.q: What does Mahima want to drop?
qa.a: The Sunday test series.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel about dance now?
qa.a: Mahima used to love it but now feels dread, worn out by a week with no gaps.

qa.q: Why is a free Sunday afternoon not a waste for Mahima?
qa.a: Rest lets the mind recover and take in what was learnt, so study and mood can improve, as Saurabh found on lazy Sundays.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel concerned and protective, and glad Mahima trusted him to help talk to Papa.

grounding: A teenager with no rest in the week feels flat and resentful and asks for free time to recover.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: Okay, Darshan, since you're writing about toppers for the school magazine, here's the real version. I'm Keerthana, Class 11. My week is school till 3:30, coaching from 4 to 8, tests on weekends, and dance on Sunday morning because Amma already paid for the year. I haven't had one empty afternoon since June. At first I felt proud. Now I mostly feel flat, like a phone on low battery that never charges. I snap at Amma, then feel guilty. Some nights my chest goes tight thinking about Monday. Last week our physics sir said something that stuck: the brain files things away when you rest. So I asked Amma if Saturday afternoons could be completely free. She was nervous, but agreed to try for a month. Two Saturdays so far. I lay on the terrace and read comics. My marks haven't dropped. I feel less like a machine.

qa.q: What hours is Keerthana at coaching?
qa.a: From 4 to 8.

qa.q: How has Keerthana's feeling about the packed schedule changed since June?
qa.a: Keerthana felt proud at first, but now feels flat, resentful and anxious, snapping at Amma and then feeling guilty.

qa.q: Why is a free Saturday afternoon not wasted time?
qa.a: Rest gives the brain time to file away what was learned and lets Keerthana recover, so marks hold and the machine feeling eases.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt agreeing to the free Saturdays?
qa.a: Amma was probably nervous about the marks but willing to try, caring more about Keerthana than the timetable.

grounding: Shows a teenager with no rest between school, coaching and activities feeling flat, resentful and anxious, and free time in the week helping the mind recover.
